title: Recognise, Remember, Respond
principle: Your body makes millions of random shapes, then copies whichever ones fit.

t: Your body can recognise a germ it has never met, and that nobody has ever met. How?
Your immune system can recognise a molecule that has never existed before — one synthesised in a laboratory last week. It cannot have been prepared for that specific thing, and yet it is.
sub: There is no room to keep a picture of everything.
The genome is not large enough to hold a receptor for every possible target. Something else must be going on.

question: How can you be ready for something nobody has ever seen?
How can a finite genome anticipate an effectively infinite set of targets?
options: Make millions of random shapes first, then pick the ones that fit
Keep a picture of every germ there is
Work out the right shape when the germ arrives
stages.outcome: Make millions of random shapes first, then pick the ones that fit
note: Guess before you look. One of these is a mechanism you have already met, in a different world.
Commit. Note that the winning strategy here is the same one that produced the beetles.

stages.label: What happens next?
captions: Millions of defence cells, each with a different random shape on it.
A germ arrives. Almost none of the cells fit it.
A few happen to fit. Those few are told to copy themselves.
Now there are millions of the ones that fit, and the germ is in trouble.
Some are kept afterwards. Next time it is quick.
t: Watch what happens when a germ arrives and only a few cells happen to match it.
Follow one encounter from a random starting population to a specific response.
after: The right cells were already there. They just got copied.
Nothing was designed in response to the germ. The matching cells existed beforehand and were selected and amplified — which is a mechanism you have run before.

stages.label: Work out which mechanism this is
captions: Variation: each lymphocyte carries a randomly assembled receptor. Millions of distinct specificities.
The variation is heritable: a cell's daughters carry its receptor.
Differential proliferation: only cells whose receptor binds the antigen are stimulated to divide.
Three conditions, all satisfied. The population shifts to match the threat.
Burnet called it clonal selection, and named it after Darwin deliberately.
t: Read each step and work out what mechanism you are looking at before the last caption tells you.
Each step states one condition. Identify the mechanism before reaching the end — you have operated it twice already, in a different world.
after: It is natural selection, running inside you, over days.

It is Darwinian selection on a cell population, on a timescale of days. Burnet's 1957 clonal selection theory was an explicit application of the same three conditions, and it is why the immune system can meet a molecule that has never existed.

t: Your body makes millions of random shapes, then copies whichever ones fit.
This is clonal selection: random receptors made in advance, and the ones that happen to bind are the ones that multiply.
Clonal selection. Receptor diversity is generated by random recombination before any antigen is encountered; antigen then selects and expands the clones that bind it.

Variety is generated by V(D)J recombination — a controlled, deliberate rearrangement of gene segments in each developing lymphocyte, producing on the order of 10¹¹ possible specificities from a few hundred segments. That is the same combinatorial trick as the four-letter alphabet, applied to shapes instead of sequence.
sub: Which is exactly what happened to the beetles.
Variation, heritability, differential success — the same three conditions you switched on and off in the beetle simulation.
The ones kept afterwards are memory cells, and they are why a second encounter is fast enough that you never feel ill.

Affinity maturation then runs a second round of the same process: memory B cells mutate their receptors at high rate and the best binders are selected again, so the response improves across encounters. Selection inside a body, over weeks, producing measurable optimisation.

q: Were the right cells made because the germ arrived?
Are matching lymphocytes produced in response to the antigen?
In what sense is the antigen not instructive?
options: No — they were already there, and the germ picked them out
Yes, the body designs a cell to fit each germ
Yes, the germ teaches the cells what shape to be
why: The cells with the right shape were made at random, before the germ ever arrived. All the germ did was find them — and then they copied themselves.

The repertoire is generated in advance and randomly. Antigen selects from what already exists; it does not instruct anything to change. This is exactly the distinction you drew about antibiotic resistance, in a different system.

The instructive theory — antigen acting as a template for antibody shape — was the leading account into the 1950s and was displaced by clonal selection. The decisive consideration was the same one that settles the resistance question: the specificity exists before the encounter, and the encounter only amplifies it.

t: It means your body was ready for a germ that did not exist yet.

Every new virus that has ever emerged met an immune system already carrying lymphocytes able to bind it, by chance, because the repertoire was generated without reference to what was coming. A defence built by anticipating specific threats would fail against every novel one; a defence built on random variation plus selection does not need to anticipate anything.
